options.A: Longer contexts per request

options.A: TPOT: each output token gets much faster

options.A: Serving updates the weights after every request
options.B: One failed GPU stalls a whole synchronized training job, so teams checkpoint often
options.C: Training GPUs must exchange gradients every step, so the network and stragglers matter as much as the chips
options.D: Training needs several times the memory per parameter (gradients and optimizer state)

options.A: Set the attention weights above the diagonal to 0 after the weighted average has been taken
options.B: Add −∞ to scores above the diagonal before softmax, so future positions get exactly 0 weight
options.C: Delete the future tokens from the input, so each position runs on a shorter sequence
options.D: Multiply the values of future tokens by 0.5, so they count for half in the weighted average

options.A: Total tokens per second rise a lot, each user's TPOT rises a little, and KV memory caps how many users fit
options.B: Total throughput stays the same, since the GPU is already busy; each user just gets 64 times slower
options.C: Each user's TPOT stays exactly the same until compute runs out, and throughput rises 64 times
options.D: Both total throughput and each user's TPOT improve, since the GPU is busier and works more efficiently per token

options.A: Quantizing to 8-bit: half the bytes per tick and room for twice the caches
options.B: Lowering the temperature: fewer candidate tokens per step, so each tick is faster
options.C: Raising the batch size: more users share each weight read, so each user's TPOT drops
options.D: Adding GPUs (tensor parallelism): more bandwidth per tick and more room for caches

options.A: There is no difference in what the model learns: both are lowest at p = 1, so −ln p is just convention
options.B: −ln p is cheaper to compute on a GPU than a subtraction across the whole vocabulary
options.C: −ln p grows without limit as p → 0, so confident wrong answers are punished hard; 1 − p caps the penalty at 1
options.D: 1 − p can go negative when the model is very confident, which would reward a wrong answer instead of punishing it

options.A: Stores past conversations on the server so the model can recall them in a later session
options.B: Adds a second, smaller model that tracks the conversation and hands the main model one turn at a time
options.C: Rewrites the user's prompt into a fixed question format, the one the base model saw most in pre-training
options.D: Wraps each turn in special tokens like <|user|> and flattens the messages into one string to continue

options.A: A snapshot read: each transaction sees only what committed before it, never later writes
options.B: A dead-letter queue: future tokens are parked to one side and processed after the current one finishes
options.C: Rate limiting: each token may only attend to a fixed number of others per step
options.D: A load balancer: each token is routed only to the attention heads that are free

options.A: Both run at the same temperature, so the probabilities they compute come out identical
options.B: The mask makes each position see only itself and earlier positions, exactly as during generation
options.C: They don't match exactly; a short extra training phase adjusts the model so generation roughly agrees
options.D: Generation quietly retrains the model after each token so it stays in step with training

options.A: Each tick reads half the weight bytes, and the freed memory holds more KV caches for a bigger batch
options.B: The model needs fewer layers and a smaller vocabulary, so each decode tick has less work to do in total
options.C: Prompts and answers get shorter, since 8-bit weights produce more compact tokens
options.D: Temperature can drop and sampling can be skipped, since 8-bit logits are already sharp

options.A: Order doesn't matter; the cache matches any shared stretch of text wherever it appears in the prompt

options.A: A write-through cache in front of a database: every new prompt is written to the cache and to disk
